task: Escribe 80–100 palabras sobre alguien que te enseñó algo importante: qué aprendiste y cómo.
paragraphs: Until I was twenty-five, my cooking skills were limited to toast, pasta with tomato sauce and, on special occasions, an omelette that was usually burnt. I had always lived with my parents or with flatmates who cooked, so I had never needed to learn.

Everything changed when I got a job in a small town in Wales. I rented a flat on my own, and the nearest takeaway was twenty minutes away by car. After two weeks of eating sandwiches every night, I was bored, tired and spending far too much money.

One evening I phoned my grandmother, who had been a wonderful cook all her life. Instead of giving me a recipe, she asked me a question: "What do you like eating?" I said lentil soup, the one she used to make when I was a child. "Then start with that," she said. Over the next hour, she explained everything slowly while I wrote notes: how to chop an onion, why you should never rush the garlic, how to know when the lentils were ready.
My first soup was too salty, and the second was too thick. But the third one tasted almost like hers. I was so proud that I sent her a photo, and she replied with a single word: "Bravo."

After that, we had a "cooking call" every Sunday. She taught me how to roast a chicken, make bread and use leftovers so that nothing was wasted. I also learned that cooking is not only about food. It is about patience, about paying attention, and about sharing.

My grandmother died two years ago. I still have the notebook from those calls, with her advice written in my untidy handwriting. Whenever I make lentil soup, I can hear her voice saying, "Don't rush the garlic."
